newsitem.title: USA: Fed alumni see continued vigilance, no rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Fed alumni see continued vigilance, no rate hike.

text.p: While Federal Reserve leaders seem as vigilant as ever for inflation omens, current economic and political conditions rule out an interest rate hike at next Tuesday's policy meeting, former Fed officials said.

Whether the Fed has kept its focus on preemptive strikes against inflation or shifted to a new theory advocating more tolerance of price growth during economic expansions, recent data suggest no action is needed, ex-Fed officials said.

"Both approaches come up with the same conclusion. There's no indication that inflation is heating up or out of control and the Fed can live with the current situation," said former Fed Governor Robert Heller.

The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets next Tuesday and Fed alumni expect no increase in the 5.25 percent federal funds rate, already 2.65 percentage points above the core Consumer Price Index over the last 12 months.

"I really don't see any immediate pressure to act. We've got a pretty balanced economic picture, with no sectors that are really overloaded," said Heller, now executive vice president at Fair Isaac and Co in San Rafael, California.

At an annual monetary policy conference last month in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, central bankers debated a new theory dubbed "opportunistic disinflation" that seeks to overload progress toward lower inflation in times of economic weakness.
This differs from a traditional Fed policy geared toward slowing the economy through higher interest rates when spurts in growth threaten to stoke faster inflation.

While some Fed officials may consider the new theory during current policy deliberations, the central bank remains committed to squashing inflation whenever it appears, said former Fed Governor John LaWare.
"I don't think the Fed has taken its eye off the inflation concern," said LaWare, now with the Alliance for the Commonwealth in Boston.
Like Heller, LaWare sees the economy slowing on its own in coming months as consumer spending and auto sales taper off.
"My personal view is the third quarter will be slower than the second and the fourth quarter is liable to be significantly slower," LaWare said.
Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew a robust 4.8 percent in the second quarter, well above the 2.0- to 2.5-percent range many economists consider the maximum without faster inflation.
But many analysts forecast GDP growth well below 3.0 percent in the third quarter, which would minimize any increase in inflation.
That scenario would also help the Fed avoid falling behind inflation as it has in many previous economic cycles, LaWare said.
"In the past the Fed has always worried: 'Did we wait too long to tighten?' I really don't see that happening this time," he added.
With the economy sending only modest inflation signals, the November 5 presidential and Congressional elections take on added significance as the Fed debates interest rates, ex-officials said.

While current Fed leaders vehemently deny politics influence monetary policy, the departed officials maintain the closeness of the elections will help convince FOMC members to hold off on raising rates next week.
"There's nothing in it for them to do it now," said Michael Belongia, University of Mississippi professor, who worked for 10 years as an economist at the St. Louis Fed.
If Fed leaders find it necessary to raise interest rates, FOMC meetings on November 13, eight days after the elections, and December 17 offer more politically palatable timing.
"I would be very surprised if the Fed does anything about interest rates before the election," LaWare said. "That would just open them up to all kinds of (political) attacks."
